messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 49-year-old architect who came to treatment after more than a year of trying to contain a reaction he could neither explain clearly nor outrun. He is married and still working, but he described moving through most days as if he were “bracing” for something. The trauma began when he witnessed a violent assault at close range outside a construction site he was visiting for work. He had stepped out near the service entrance at the end of a meeting, and the scene unfolded with sudden, shocking force: shouting, the unmistakable sound of bodies colliding, and the metallic, sour smell around the loading area mixing with what he later only called “that smell.” He remembers freezing as another man was beaten. What has stayed with him most is not a clean story but fragments with too much immediacy and too little order. He knows what happened, but when he tries to describe it he loses words, goes silent, and says the pieces come “all at once” rather than in sequence.

In the weeks afterward, David found that reminders reached him before he had time to think. News footage showing violence, a confrontation on the street, even a smell at a job site that resembled the odor from that loading area could bring on a wave of nausea and the immediate sense that the event was happening again. At those moments the memory did not feel like something from the past. He would be back there in his body, disoriented, unable to place what came first and what came next. Because these reminders landed so abruptly, he began entering conference rooms, restaurants, and client buildings already on guard. He would position himself with his back to a wall, scan for exits the moment he walked in, and jolt hard at ordinary noises, as if his body had learned that any setting could turn without warning.

As he tried to make sense of his reaction, David had come to believe there was something about him that had allowed the event to happen in front of him. He did not say this logically; he knew he had not caused the assault. But he felt marked by some personal failing, as if he lacked whatever other men have that lets them stop bad things. What frightened him most was the conviction that he could not prevent terrible events and would not see them coming. That belief sharpened his vigilance everywhere. In his office he now chooses the chair that lets him see the door and the whole room, and during site visits he automatically maps exit routes before he can focus on the plans in front of him.

Those same beliefs also seemed to make the world fill with reminders. Because he was certain that danger could break through anywhere and that he would again be helpless, signs of possible violence pulled his attention immediately: raised voices on the sidewalk, rough joking between contractors, footage playing on a waiting room television. Smells registered too quickly and too intensely. He noticed them, then his stomach turned, and the whole environment took on the charge of a warning. His wife has told him that other people seem able to let these things pass, but David feels set apart from them, as though he is living in a world where threat is always closer than anyone else understands.

Once his body goes on alert, the memories become even harder to keep in the past. If he is already scanning a room, tracking exits, and sitting rigidly with his back protected, any abrupt sound or movement can tip him into reliving. He then struggles even more to describe what happened, because the memory arrives as sensation and alarm rather than a coherent account. He leaves meetings remembering only flashes. On several occasions at work, after hearing shouting on a nearby floor or catching a related smell near building materials, he became so jumpy and nauseated that he had to step out, then found himself replaying the assault in fragments for the rest of the day.

Over time the vigilance has narrowed his life and fed the problem it is meant to solve. Because he is constantly checking rooms and monitoring other people, he is primed to notice exactly the kinds of cues that set him off. Each new startle, each scan for exits, each effort to stay positioned against a wall seems to confirm that danger is near, and the reminders come faster. At home he sits in restaurants only if he can face the entrance; at work he avoids parts of active sites where smells are strong or tempers run high. Colleagues have noticed he is more distracted during presentations, and his wife says he is physically present but far away.

He sought help after a client meeting in which a loud argument broke out in the hallway outside the conference room. David felt nauseated immediately, began searching for the exits before anyone else had even paused, and then lost the thread of where he was, caught in the sense that the assault was happening again. He was shaken by how quickly he could disappear from the present and by how impossible it still felt to put the original event into words. What he fears most is that this means he will never be able to trust himself in the world again; what he hopes, cautiously, is that he might learn how to be in a room without feeling he has to survive it.
